INTRODUCTION
Excavations were carried out in the area northeast of the theater between 1-19 April 2024. Eric Del Fabbro and Hannah Lents supervised excavation of trench 16A, an area within the hypothetical space of the "Marble Room’s" apodyterium. Our objective this session was to understand the nature of the Byzantine and early Modern occupation of the area, which had covered the Late Roman bath complex.

query: Marble room secondary use in Theater's Northeast
document:
Conclusion
The Session I excavation of Trench 15A in the Northeast of Theater provided more information about the secondary use of the marble room uncovered in the 2021 and 2022 excavations of the area as well as exposed more of Wall 24 from Trenches 14B and 15B. During the end of the Late Roman period (6th c. AD or slightly later), the area served as a dump for both large quantities of ceramic material and building material. At some point in the 6th c. or possibly the 7th c. AD, the upper part of Wall 24 was destroyed. The area was then potentially abandoned for some centuries until it was used again in possibly the 12th c.

query: Cache of semi-intact Dressel 2-4 Amphoras in 2022 excavation
document: Object C2022-7: Dressel 2-4 Amphora with Dipinto on shoulder (late 1st cent. BCE – 1st cent. CE). The central body of this amphora was excavated as part of NET 16C in 2022, and its dating and typology have accordingly been discussed elsewhere. The extraction of the upper body, neck, and handles of the amphora from the wall of the drain in 16B during this excavation season, however, has allowed for the realization that this amphora in fact appears to have been purposefully encased within the construction of the wall. It would therefore appear that this amphora, and perhaps the rest of the cache excavated in 2022, were employed in their semi-intact state as some form of cover for Drain 6.

query: What are the relationships between drains 5, 6, and 9 at Deposit 177?
document:
SUGGESTIONS FOR FUTURE EXCAVATION
Several questions remain concerning the relationship of the three drains (5, 6, 9) to one another, as well as to the chronology of the pipes and roadways once running above. The nature and extent of disturbance that destroyed the pipes and robbed the drain in this area is also left unexplained. The abutment of the two subsidiary drains of different construction also warrants further investigation (does the disuse of one, for instance, correspond to the creation of the other?). Some of these questions might be answered by the excavation of what remains of the eastern balk of Deposit 177 north of Drain 9.

By the end of Session I, excavations in Trench 2C demonstrated that robbing trench 1 continues westward and runs the length of the trench. query: Roman coins found in Pit 1 dating back to Theodosius I and Arcadius
document: Pit 1 has a diameter of.96 and a depth of.552. This pit yielded 50 coins, including several of the salus republice type issued by Theodosius I and Arcadius (383 – 408 AD) and the Concordia auggg type of Arcadius (395 – 408 AD). Many of the coins in the pits were illegible, but the group from context 38 seems to include a few coins of the minimus denomination (5th – 6th c. AD), which is consistent with our general pottery chronologies and the extended circulation of late Roman bronze coinage over centuries (see Guest, Peter. 2012. query: Ancient activities in Shop 1 Rear excavated room
document:
Conclusion
The excavation activities of this session have raised more questions about ancient activities in the room than they have answered. The primary problem that is raised by the types of contexts in Shop 1 Rear so far excavated is that there are no clearly identified floor levels, and therefore no clear idea of activities within the room during different use phases. Most of the deposits represent fill events rather than occupation phases. Various construction phases also severely disrupted earlier levels and therefore caused a high degree of fragmentation of deposits within the space of the room.

query: Worked stone framing elderly woman's head archaeological find
document: The primary inhumation (1025) was that of an elderly woman, oriented W-E, laid supine with her head elevated facing east and turned slightly to the south. The head was framed by a worked stone to the north and tiles to the west and south. The mandible was likely supported by a rock, which later fell out of place and came to rest on the sternum. The shoulders were elevated and the humeri drawn in so that they rested directly against the anterior-lateral aspects of the rib cage. The forearms were bent at the elbow and crossed over the chest with the left forearm over the right.

query: Byzantine corridor activity during AD 802-1058
document:
Middle Byzantine (AD 802-1058)
Corridor
In its earliest phase this area seems to have been open and little used. Neither Wall 156 to the north (dated by Bennett in Session I to the late third quarter of the 13th century), nor Wall 20 to the south had yet been constructed. The presence of faunal remains and construction material in several fill layers (Contexts 682, 702, 705, 707, 710, 718, 722, 723, 724, 725), the earliest of which (725) is dated by pottery to the early 12th century, attests to mixed activities in this area, although relative to later, Frankish contexts these were fairly sterile of finds.

query: Middle 13th century church foundation trench
document:
Conclusion
Corridor
We met the goal of finding a foundation trench for Wall 20, and it currently dates the construction of the church to the middle of the 13th century (based on coin 2015-151 from context 743). There seems to have been a gap in activity in the area between the 12th (latest context 702) and the mid-13th centuries. Further excavation could address this apparent gap and better define the use of the space in pre-Frankish levels. Following the construction of the church, the area immediately adjacent to its north wall became a popular location for inhumation.

query: Frankish building abandonment in 15th century
document:
Frankish Period (14th-15th Century CE)
In our area, there is evidence forabandonment at the end of the Frankish period in the later fifteenth century. Most of the Frankish layers remain unexcavated, but some tentative conclusions can be drawn. A room of a Frankish building, the extent of which is still undetermined, fell out of use in the fifteenth century at which point it began to degrade slowly. Water was allowed to permeate the roof of this structure and dissolved the clay used to bond the roof to the upper structure of the walls. The melted clay leaked between the stones of the walls and onto the surface beneath them (deposits 131 and 132).

query: Late Classical to Early Hellenistic ritual activity in Korinth
document: It is interesting that this ritual activity was concentrated in the same area from the Late Classical period down into the Early Hellenistic period. This quiet interior space and ritual transcended the political turbulence that marred Korinth in the late 4th century BCE. The most contested of battlegrounds, Korinth hosted the armies of Phillip II and his son Alexander (338-323), the Antigonids (323-308), the Ptolemies (308-304), and then, under Demetrios Poliorketes, a second period of Antigonid hegemony. Confronted by chronic war and (forced) foreign rule, it is possible that this ritualized space, which had definite roots in the Classical period, served as a discreet assertion of longstanding Greek identity in the face of a new, Macedonian regime.

query: Transition between Late Byzantine and early Frankish Periods in Korinth
document:
Our latest levels (Deposits 1219, 1212, 1221) date to the Frankish period on firm ceramic grounds, but still feature sherds of Byzantine fine ware. It is likely that in these deposits, we are glimpsing the transition between the Late Byzantine and early Frankish Periods. This scenario serves as a reminder that the material culture at Korinth did not alter instantly in the wake of the Fourth Crusade; the change was gradual. The ceramic record reveals more of an ease into the Frankish era, with vessels categorized as "Byzantine" being used well into the mid-late 13th century CE.
If politics changed overnight, it appears that the ceramics—and likely other aspects of daily life—did not.

query: Stratigraphy analysis of Northwestern Quadrant at Nezi site in 2013
document: This is the final report for the second session of excavation at Nezi, 2013. Our excavation area encompassed the area between walls 1007, 918, 945 and pit 870 in the first half of the session (hereafter referred to as "South Section"). During the third week, our efforts focused on the quadrant north of 918 and west of W5218 (bounded by the Turkish building) (hereafter referred to as "Northwestern Quadrant"). Our excavation goals are to elucidate the stratigraphy of these areas and the function of the architectural features. With this, we hoped to find uncontaminated habitation levels that would help us to determine the chronology of human interaction in this area.

query: Destruction and non-destruction debris in Northwestern Quadrant
document: Because of the nature of the depositional material and the heavy pitting and dumping, we were unable to identify discrete chronological phases in this section. query: West Corridor steps and threshold associated with fifth-century fill

2. The steps to the west ascend to a broad floor, in part with patches of cement suggesting that it was once paved (floor 5). The floor extends well to the west. The fill overlying both the steps and the cement floor is 5th c. in date, Basket 4018 (Lot 2011-56).

3. The steps of the West Corridor end at the north in a long threshold block (top +61.51); beneath it is an earlier step block which is oriented somewhat more to the SE-NW. This step lower was covered by Basket 4018 (Lot 2011-56).
